BMX5102 Business Analytics · Week 4 in-class assignment

The Promise Olist Can Keep

Peh Shao Hong (A0077294U)

Stakeholder Head of Operations, Olist, presenting to the CEO, CFO and Chief Commercial Officer Dataset 99,441 orders · 3,095 sellers · Sept 2016 – Oct 2018, of which Jan 2017 – Aug 2018 is usable Joined to an event calendar, Open-Meteo weather, BrasilAPI holidays, ANP diesel prices, IBGE boundaries, SEC filings

About this page

This is a coursework submission for BMX5102, on visualisation: one research objective, five questions, and a set of charts for each, with a short write-up of what they show. The five questions run in one line, promise → stage → distance → stress → cost. The first sizes the gap, the second and third locate it, the fourth tests it under load, the fifth prices it.

The objective, the questions, the role and the audience were fixed before the data was opened, so that the executive team can trust the findings were not chosen to fit a conclusion already held. Every chart here is generated in Python with matplotlib, straight out of the notebook the analysis was done in.

Six external sources were brought in as the questions demanded them. Each one is tested against the data in the section that uses it, and three of them are ruled out. That is deliberate: a source that fails to explain something is still evidence.

How this was made

This is the order the work actually happened in. The steps marked in red are the ones that looped.

  1. The framing came first. Role, audience, one-sentence objective, five questions, and a table of rejected candidates, all written before a single row was read.
  2. Everything was built in a Python notebook. Load the nine Olist CSV files, then check them before trusting them: that check is Step 0 below.
  3. Ten gaps, ten decisions, one clean table. Each gap found in Step 0 got one decision, applied once. Two of them (the midnight promise date, the impossible timestamp sequences) were only found after a first pass produced numbers that did not add up.
  4. Each question answered once, with one chart. The chart decided the answer, not the other way round. The August 2018 promise cut was checked for a data-cutoff artefact before it was believed.
  5. The event calendar was tested, not assumed. Six supplied events were written down with what each should look like in the data, then checked. Three matched, one half-matched, and the worst episode in the data had no event at all.
  6. Weather looked like the cause, and was not. Pooled, wet weeks were far later. Held within each state and month, the effect vanished. The first chart was thrown away and the test rebuilt so the confound could not hide.
  7. More sources, more tests. National holidays for a working-day view, ANP diesel prices, the Correios service ceiling, Mercado Livre’s filings and Olist’s own deal history. Diesel and holidays were ruled out too; the last two shaped the recommendation.
  8. The notebook was rebuilt with several charts per question and maps. A corridor matrix, three-map sequences, a stress curve and sampled routes were added once the single charts had shown where to look.
  9. Then out of the notebook, onto this page. Each chart as it was drawn, with the write-up beside it.

Research objective

To understand how reliably Olist’s delivery network performs as demand rises and shifts across the country, in order to decide what delivery standard Olist can commit to as it scales.

Question 1: promise
How does the gap between promised and actual delivery behave, across orders and over time?
Decides how much slack the promise needs
Question 2: stage
Where in the journey does delivery time vary most, seller handling or carrier transit?
Decides whose problem it is
Question 3: distance
How does reliability change with the distance goods travel, and does the promise stretch with it?
Decides one standard or tiered
Question 4: stress
How does performance behave when volume surges, and does every region absorb it equally?
Decides the Black Friday plan
Question 5: cost
How does satisfaction behave as delivery moves from ahead of the promise to behind it?
Sizes the whole investment

First, does the data hold up?

The checks that have to pass before any chart on this page means anything.

Nine Olist files, one marketplace, two years, and seven external sources pulled in as the questions demanded them. Every order is a row with five timestamps: purchase, approval, hand-off to the carrier, delivery to the customer, and the date the customer was promised. Reliability on this page is measured from those five fields, so it is worth knowing where they are silent, and what was joined to them.

Integrity checks, all passing

  • Every order id is unique, and every order’s customer id resolves to a customer
  • Every promised delivery date is a date at midnight, so lateness is compared on the calendar day, not the timestamp
  • Every seller and customer zip prefix used for distance resolves to at least one coordinate
  • Order status is one of eight values; 97% are delivered, the rest shipped, cancelled, unavailable, invoiced, processing, created or approved
  • Purchase dates run 4 Sept 2016 to 17 Oct 2018; the last delivery is 17 Oct 2018
  • All 27 states appear on both the seller and the customer side
  • Weather: 760 days for each of 12 capitals, no gaps; those 12 states hold 93.5% of delivered orders
  • Diesel: every one of the 27 states present in every survey week; the strike week is flagged by ANP as an 85% drop in stations with fuel
  • Boundaries: 27 polygons, one per state, matched to the two-letter codes used in the Olist files
  • Every fact in the strategy file carries a source URL, and every figure quoted on this page was read from that source

What the checks found, and what was done

  • The series is thin at both ends. 2016 holds a few hundred orders and Sept–Oct 2018 holds twenty. Everything on this page uses purchase months January 2017 to August 2018.
  • Eight delivered orders have no delivery date, and two have no carrier date. Dropped. A delivery with no date cannot be measured.
  • 189 delivered orders have an impossible sequence, delivered before hand-off or handed off before purchase. They are timestamp errors and are dropped from the seller-versus-carrier split only.
  • Some orders carry several reviews, and one review id can sit on several orders. The latest review per order is kept.
  • About 1% of orders have items from more than one seller. The first item’s seller stands for the order.
  • There is no road distance and no carrier name. Distance is straight-line between zip-prefix centroids; the carrier leg is hand-off to delivery, one block, with no split between line-haul and last mile.
1

How does the gap between promised and actual delivery behave, across orders and over time?

A question of magnitude. It decides how much slack the promise needs, and how aggressive the customer-facing date can be.

Key findings

The promise is padded, and the padding halved in 2018.

  • 10 days to deliver against 23 promised, so 79% of parcels arrive a week or more early and only 6.8% arrive late
  • Lateness is episodic, not chronic: 3 to 5% in a normal month, 12% at Black Friday 2017 and 19% in March 2018
  • Median slack fell from 13 days to 7 by August 2018, and the 10th percentile now sits on the promise line

What it does not answer: whether the shorter August promise was a deliberate commercial choice or a formula change. The data shows the cut and its effect, not the decision behind it.

The customer is told about 23 days and receives the parcel in about 10. Four orders in five arrive a week or more early. The 6.8% late rate is what survives that buffer, and among the late orders the median is 7 days late and the 90th percentile 22. The buffer is doing almost all of the work.

It is not a steady state. Two episodes account for the spikes: the two weeks after Black Friday 2017, and six weeks from mid-February 2018. A smaller bump in April 2017 coincides with the start of the Correios postal strike. Outside those, the late rate holds near 3 to 5% for eighteen months.

The August 2018 number is the one to carry into the boardroom. Deliveries that month were the fastest in the data, a median of 7 days, yet lateness rose to 6.2%, because the promise had been cut to 13 days. Median slack went from 12 to 14 days through 2017 to 7 days in August 2018, and the 10th percentile now sits on the line. That is the buffer Olist carries into Black Friday 2018, and it is half of what it had at Black Friday 2017.

Two checks were run before believing that. First, the cut is not a data-cutoff artefact: the promise across all August orders, delivered or not, is the same 13 days, and only 2.5% of August orders were still undelivered when the file ends. Second, the calendar-versus-working-day view, built from national holidays, shows working time is 63 to 68% of calendar time in every month, including the Carnival and Christmas months. Late orders in March 2018 were still five to six working days behind the promise, the same as in a calm month. Holidays do not explain the spikes; they only make them look a little larger.

2

Where in the journey does delivery time vary most, seller handling or carrier transit?

A question of ownership. It decides whose problem it is: seller SLA enforcement, carrier contracts, or Olist taking control of fulfilment.

Key findings

The delivery problem is a carrier-tail problem. Seller handling is tight, independent, and did not move through any crisis.

  • Carrier transit carries 86% of the variance; on late orders the carrier leg runs a median 26 days against 7 normally
  • Seller handling is a median 2.2 days, p90 6.4, and correlates 0.04 with the carrier leg
  • 9% of orders leave after the shipping limit; those are late 21% of the time against 5%, and the top tenth of sellers produce 77% of the misses

What it does not answer: which carrier, or which part of the carrier leg. The data has no carrier field and cannot split line-haul from last mile. Question 3 is the proxy.

The journey has two legs and they behave nothing alike. The seller’s leg, purchase to carrier hand-off, is short and tight: a median of 2.2 days, a 90th percentile of 6.4, and it improved slightly through 2018. The carrier’s leg, hand-off to doorstep, is a median of 7.1 days with a 90th percentile of 18.9 and a 95th of 24. Carrier transit carries 86% of the variance in delivery time, and the two legs are independent of each other.

Late orders make the point sharper. On an order that arrives late, the seller leg is a median 3.5 days, one day slower than normal. The carrier leg is 26 days, nearly four times normal. And in the two crisis months, the share of late orders that involved any seller miss at all falls below a fifth: the network broke with the seller having done its part.

Sellers are not blameless, but their problem is a different shape. About 9% of orders are handed to the carrier after the shipping deadline on the order item, and those orders are late 21% of the time against 5% when the deadline is met. Roughly 28% of late orders involve such a miss. The misses are concentrated: the top tenth of sellers produce 77% of them, and 107 sellers with twenty or more orders miss on more than a fifth of theirs. That is a Seller Success task, and it costs nothing in logistics budget.

What it cannot say is why the carrier leg fails. There is no carrier name in the data and no scan between hand-off and delivery, so line-haul and last mile are one block. Question 3 uses distance as the proxy: if reliability degrades with distance while seller handling does not, the failure is in the carrier network.

3

How does reliability change with the distance goods travel, and does the promise stretch with it?

A question of geography. It decides whether one national delivery standard is achievable, or whether standards must be tiered by corridor.

Key findings

A national standard is already tiered in practice. The decision is whether to admit it, write it on the corridor matrix, and set it at the 90th percentile.

  • Slack grows with distance, from about 8 days under 50 km to 13 beyond 1,500 km, yet the late rate still rises from 4% to 12% because the tail grows faster than the median
  • Seller handling does not change with distance at all (correlation 0.02); the whole distance effect is the carrier leg
  • Rio de Janeiro is 12% late at 394 km, the same rate as Bahia at 1,400 km: a last-mile problem, not line-haul

What it does not answer: what happens inside the carrier leg. Distance is straight-line between zip centroids, and a parcel to Salvador may route through three hubs this data never sees.

Distance does what it should. The median delivery goes from 5 days under 50 km to 18 beyond 1,500 km, and the promise goes from 14 to 32. The promise stretches more than the delivery, so median slack widens with distance. On the median, the network is over-promising nowhere.

The tail is another matter. The 90th percentile goes from 11 days to 34 across the same bands, and beyond 1,500 km it crosses the promise line. The late rate rises from 4% to 12% not because the typical parcel slows down more than the promise allows, but because the slowest tenth do. Seller handling is flat across every band, so all of that tail sits in the carrier leg.

The maps and the corridor matrix add what a distance chart hides. The far North, Amazonas and Amapá, is the slowest region and almost never late, because its promise runs past 40 days. The Northeast is late at every distance. And Rio de Janeiro is as late as Bahia at a quarter of the distance, with a carrier median of 8 days for a 400 km hop. That is a last-mile signature: the parcel reaches the city and then stalls.

The working-day comparison closes one door. In working days, using national holidays, Olist already promises at or above the Correios PAC service ceiling on every band, ten working days under 50 km and twenty-six beyond 3,000. Olist is not promising faster than the carrier’s own standard. It is promising slower, and the tail still breaks it. The 2018 route-level Correios tables are not public, so the comparison uses the stated ceiling and is indicative only.

4

How does performance behave when order volume surges, and does every region absorb it equally?

A question of stress. It decides what peak capacity to plan for Black Friday 2018, and where to pre-position it.

The supplied calendar names three logistics shocks inside the data: the Correios strike from 26 April 2017, Black Friday on 24 November 2017, and the truckers’ strike of 21 to 31 May 2018. The data itself adds a fourth, February to March 2018, that the calendar does not cover. Each is tested below; then weather, diesel and volume itself are tested as candidate causes.

Event or candidate causeWhat it should look likeWhat the data shows
Recession, then recoveryThin early data, then accelerationConfirmed. A few hundred orders in 2016, then growth every month of 2017.
Correios strike, Apr 2017Longer transit and more late orders in late April and MayConfirmed, modest. Orders on the road when it began were about 8% late against 3%; carrier p90 rose to 23 days; seller handling unchanged.
Black Friday, 24 Nov 2017Volume spike in week 47, lateness afterConfirmed. Olist’s peak day ran at 7.5× a normal day, matching the market’s 7.9×. Lateness tripled, and the damage landed outside São Paulo.
Truckers’ strike, 21–31 May 2018Late deliveries and low reviews for orders placed 15 May to 10 JuneHalf confirmed. The week before, 12% late; orders in transit, 15% late with reviews near 4.0. The window as a whole shows no rise, because the promise went to 37 days and orders halved.
H1 2018 demand +12%Logistics hit harder than demandAt Olist, demand dipped for one week and recovered by mid-June; its own H1 growth was 182%, far above market.
WeatherWet transit weeks, longer carrier legOnly when pooled. Within state and month the effect is nil, and Feb–Mar 2018 was not unusually wet where lateness was worst.
DieselCost pressure, slower or dearer freightFreight charged did not follow diesel; lateness does not track price. Context for the strike, not a cause.
Volume itselfMore orders, longer tailNo. Calm weeks show no relationship, and 2018 weeks are bigger and faster than 2017 weeks.
February–March 2018Nothing in the calendarThe worst episode: 19% late in March, carrier p90 up to 34 days, no surge, seller handling flat, not the weather, not diesel, not holidays. Starts the week of Carnival, peaks two to three weeks later. The one shock the promise did not absorb, and the one still unexplained.

Key findings

Padding the promise works and costs sales. The network fails under a supply shock, not a demand one, and it fails outside São Paulo.

  • At Black Friday 2017 volume ran at 2.4× baseline; seller handling barely moved, carrier p90 went from 16 to 26 days, and lateness rose three to five times in every region except São Paulo
  • February–March 2018 was worse with no surge at all: 19% late, carrier p90 34 days, the Northeast and North a third late. Weather, diesel, holidays and volume have each been tested and ruled out
  • In the truckers’ strike Olist pushed the promise to 37 days, lateness fell under 1%, and weekly orders halved before recovering in three weeks

What it does not answer: what happened in February and March 2018. Every candidate on this page has been eliminated; the episode is described but not explained, and the executive team should ask the carrier.

Only one of the four shocks was a surge. In the two weeks after Black Friday 2017, orders ran at 353 a day against 149 in the autumn baseline. Seller handling barely moved, 7.0 to 7.4 days at the 90th percentile. Carrier transit went from 16 to 26 days at the 90th percentile, and the late rate from 5% to 16%. São Paulo absorbed it, 4% to 8%. The rest of the Southeast went to 24%, the South to 17%, the Northeast to 28%.

The other three shocks had no surge. February to March 2018 was the worst episode in the data and it happened at ordinary volume: order counts matched January, seller handling was flat, and the carrier tail ran to 34 days. The North and Northeast went a third late; São Paulo stayed under a tenth. The stress curve makes the general point: across seventy weeks, volume and the carrier tail are unrelated once the shock weeks are set aside, and the 2018 weeks are both larger and faster than 2017’s.

Each candidate cause was tested rather than assumed. Rain looked like one until it was held within state and month, at which point the wetter half of orders was exactly as late as the drier half in 236 state-months, and February to March 2018 was no wetter than 2017 in São Paulo, Rio or Bahia. Diesel rose 24% from mid-2017 to the strike, but the freight Olist charges did not follow it and neither did lateness. Holidays shorten the working-day count by two at Carnival and one at Christmas, not enough to matter.

The truckers’ strike is the natural experiment the recommendation rests on. Orders placed in the week before were 12% late and orders already on the road were 15%. The week after the strike began, Olist pushed the median promise to 37 days. Lateness fell to 0.4%. Weekly orders fell from 1,837 to 954 and took three weeks to recover. Padding works, and the customer pays for it in the only currency that shows up here: fewer orders placed.

5

How does customer satisfaction behave as delivery moves from ahead of the promise to behind it?

A question of consequence. It decides what a day of unreliability costs, which sizes the whole investment.

Key findings

A late day costs two stars within a week. An early day earns nothing.

  • On-time orders score 4.29, late orders 2.27; the share of one-and-two-star reviews goes from 9% to 62%
  • The cliff starts on day one: 4.0 on the promised day, 3.7 one day late, 2.9 at two to three days, 2.1 at four to seven
  • Late and undelivered orders are a tenth of reviewed orders and half of all one-star reviews; removing lateness would lift the platform score from 4.16 to 4.29

What it does not answer: the cost in reais. Only 3% of customers reorder, so retention is a weak lever. The cost sits in marketplace ranking, and pricing it needs Mercado Livre’s seller-rating thresholds, the one external source not yet joined.

Reviews are attached to orders, not to delivery events, so this is association rather than proven cause. But the shape is hard to read any other way. From three weeks early to a few days early, the mean score sits at 4.3 and does not move. On the promised day it is 4.0. One day late, 3.7. Two to three days late, 2.9. Four to seven days late, 2.1. After that it is flat near 1.7, because there is nowhere further to fall.

Past a week late, four reviews in five are one or two stars, and late orders alone, under 7% of reviewed orders, supply 37% of all one-star reviews on delivered orders. Add the orders that were never delivered and delivery explains about half of every one-star review the platform receives. If late orders had scored like on-time ones, the platform mean would be 4.29 instead of 4.16. March 2018 alone dragged it to 3.81.

Speed matters a little even when the promise is kept. Among on-time orders, those delivered within three days score 4.48 and those that took three to four weeks score 4.0. A tenth of a star a week is small beside the cliff, but it says a long promise that is always kept is not free either.

What this cannot do is turn stars into reais. The reviewed orders carry about R$15 million of payments and late orders are 7% of it, but only 3% of customers place a second order, so lost repeat business is a small number. The real cost is the one the framing named: Mercado Livre, B2W and Via Varejo rank sellers by delivery performance, and a seller demoted on those channels loses sales this dataset never sees. Pricing that needs the marketplaces’ own rating rules, which are not joined here.

→

What to do next

One recommendation, two alternatives, and how to tell whether it worked.

Recommendation

Commit to a promise tiered by corridor and set at the 90th percentile, and put the August slack back outside São Paulo before Black Friday.

The network is fast on the median and fragile in the tail, and the tail lives in the carrier leg on the corridors out of São Paulo. The promise is the one lever the data proves works, and it has just been cut in half.

Option 1

Keep one national date, set on the median

Leave the August 2018 promise as it is: 13 days, everywhere. It is the fastest the network has ever looked and it sells.

Against it: the 10th percentile of slack is already on the line. On the 2017 pattern, a Black Friday surge would put every region outside São Paulo at 17 to 28% late, and the review cliff starts on day one.

Option 2 Recommended

Tier the promise by corridor, at the p90

Write the promise on the Question 3 corridor matrix: within São Paulo, keep the short date; to the rest of the Southeast, the South and the Centre-West, restore the 2017 slack; to the Northeast and North, set the date at the 90th percentile of the carrier leg. Hand the 107-seller miss list to Seller Success.

For it: it costs no capital, it spends slack only where the tail breaks the promise, and the strike showed it works in a week. Against it: a longer promise costs orders, and the strike week showed how many.

Option 3

Build the network now

Take control of fulfilment the way Mercado Livre did: own warehouses, cross-docking, subsidised shipping.

Against it, for now: Mercado Livre spent US$425m on shipping subsidies in 2018 and seventeen points of gross margin, and built in São Paulo, the one corridor where Olist is already reliable. Olist’s own answer came two years later and was first mile, not last. It is the 2020 answer, not the Black Friday 2018 one.

Why the p90 and not the median. Every question on this page found the same shape: a median that is fine and a tail that is not. The promise set on the median is what produced 79% of parcels arriving a week early and the slowest tenth arriving late. Setting it at the 90th percentile of each corridor is the smallest change that puts the buffer where the failures are.

Why by corridor. The corridor matrix runs from 5% late within São Paulo to 13% into the Northeast, and Rio is late at a quarter of the distance. One national number is either too loose for São Paulo, which costs sales, or too tight for everywhere else, which costs stars. The tiers already exist in the promise formula, which stretches with distance; the recommendation is to widen them at the tail.

How to tell whether it worked. Read the late rate by corridor for the two weeks after Black Friday 2018 against the same two weeks of 2017, and read it at the 90th percentile, not the mean. Read review scores by state the same way. If the Northeast and Rio still run above 20% late with the longer promise, the constraint is carrier capacity and the conversation moves to Option 3. If they fall to São Paulo’s level, the promise was the problem all along.

One caveat from Question 4. The strike showed that a longer promise halves weekly orders while it is in force. Watch the order count on the tiered corridors as closely as the late rate, because that is where the cost of this recommendation will appear.

+

What the competitor did, and what Olist did next

Not a sixth question. Two external sources that frame the CEO’s decision: whether Olist stays a software layer or extends into fulfilment.

The two sources point the same way. Mercado Livre’s answer to the reliability question was to own the network and subsidise the shipping, at a cost that a company Olist’s size could not carry in 2018. Olist’s own answer, two years later, was to buy the first mile: collection and cross-docking in São Paulo, Rio, Curitiba, Belo Horizonte and Porto Alegre. That matches the evidence here, because seller handling and hand-off are the part of the journey Olist can control, and the São Paulo corridor is where the scale is.

Neither answers the Northeast and Rio last mile, which is where most of the lateness on this page sits. That remains a carrier-contract and promise-setting question, which is why the recommendation above is about the promise and not about warehouses.

Data. The nine Olist CSV files from Kaggle, joined on order, customer, seller and zip prefix. Purchase months January 2017 to August 2018; 96,470 delivered orders with a delivery date, of which 96,281 have a valid seller-to-carrier split, 95,803 a distance and 95,824 a review. Distances are haversine between zip-prefix median coordinates.

External sources. Event calendar as supplied (Ebit/Webshoppers via PagBrasil, CEP-Research, Labsnews). Daily precipitation for twelve state capitals from the Open-Meteo historical archive. National holidays 2016 to 2018 from BrasilAPI. Weekly retail diesel prices by state from the ANP price survey. State boundaries from the IBGE malhas API. Mercado Livre figures from its 2018 Form 10-K, Q4 2017 results and the Q4 2018 earnings call. Olist funding and acquisitions from Computerworld Brasil, Exame, NeoFeed, Baguete and Bloomberg Línea; the Correios PAC and SEDEX ceilings from Olist’s own shipping guide, since the 2018 route tables are not archived.

Reading the charts. Every chart is a static matplotlib figure from the analysis notebook. Blue is the promise or the on-time case; red is late. No chart uses two y-axes; where two measures share a time axis they sit in two panels. Maps colour whole states, so the seven small coastal states are listed beside each map rather than labelled on it.

What this cannot say. There is no carrier name and no split between line-haul and last mile. Reviews attach to orders, not delivery events. The event calendar does not cover February to March 2018, and neither do weather, diesel, holidays or volume. Marketplace seller-rating rules are not joined, so Question 5 is unpriced. The data ends in August 2018; the forward view comes from the recommendation, not the five questions.
